44787374.article_content:
I have been exploring some new tools here and there. When I started watching
Primeagen
, I took a note of several tools that he was using and advocating for. One of them was tmux.
What is tmux?
#
tmux
is a terminal multiplexer. What that means is you can have many terminals in one. According to tmux wiki:
tmux is a program which runs in a terminal and allows multiple other terminal programs to be run inside it. Each program inside tmux gets its own terminal managed by tmux, which can be accessed from the single terminal where tmux is running - this called multiplexing and tmux is a terminal multiplexer.
tmux goes further by allowing you to have a lot of control over how the terminals are displayed, how they function, and how are they styled. You can have many separate windows as tabs. You can have many panes within one window. Are you working on several different projects? Then why don’t you have multiple sessions - each of them containing sets of windows and panes - all giving you access to multiple terminals. With a tool like this you no longer need to arrange multiple terminal instance windows on your desktop or using multiple workspaces for those instances - you can have it all in one place.
One additional feature that tmux boasts in is the ability to retain the terminal session upon its closure. Imagine that you have a long running process like a local server or a persistent connection like ssh session. If you were to close that window, you would lose that session and the process that was in it. Tmux has the ability to detach and attach to multiple sessions making them easier to manage and not to worry about losing it.
tmux wiki goes into detail talking about several other features of tmux:
The main uses of tmux are to:
Protect running programs on a remote server from connection drops by running them inside tmux.
Allow programs running on a remote server to be accessed from multiple different local computers.
Work with multiple programs and shells together in one terminal, a bit like a window manager.
For example:
A user connects to a remote server using ssh(1) from an xterm(1) on their work computer and run several programs. perhaps an editor, a compiler and a few shells.
They work with these programs interactively, perhaps start compiling, then close the xterm(1) with tmux and go home for the day.
They are then able to connect to the same remote server from home, attach to tmux, and continue from where they were previously.
My first tmux experience
#
The first impression of tmux didn’t leave me with much excitement of exploring what is truly possible :/ Source:
https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started
When I first started using tmux, I felt overwhelmed by the very poor default UI that it offers and the amount of options and shortcuts that I needed to know to operate it well and be productive. It took me several tries before I started to feel more or less comfortable with it.
One of the things that stood out to me right away was how dreadful UI looked. Not only it felt uninviting, but it almost felt “gatekeepy” - if you don’t know how to use it in this configuration, then might as well forget about it. But one thing that kept me going was the promise of a highly customizable terminal that I could make my own at some point.
While promising all of these amazing features, the dreadful tmux UI didn’t necessarily inspire :( Source:
https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started
Customization journey
#
To preface, I must mention that I am using
iterm2
with
Powerline10k
and
NerdFonts
. They heavily affect the final look of the tmux due to colors and icons being inherited from the iterm2 configuration. With that said, let’s get into it.
The file that is responsible for customizing tmux - its function and its look - is
.tmux.conf
. This file should be located in user’s Home folder a.k.a.
~/
. That is where tmux will be looking for it.
There are quite a few options when it comes to customizing tmux. One of the first things that I wanted to address was the
prefix
key binding. This prefix is a key combination that you would use to enter the tmux shortcut or command mode. By default, the prefix is
C-b
a.k.a.
Ctrl-b
. One of the common remaps that most people go with is to switch it to
C-a
, which is a lot easier to use. To do that, we need to add the following lines to the configuration file:
# remap prefix from 'C-b' to 'C-a'
unbind C-b
set-option -g prefix C-a
bind-key C-a send-prefix
While researching ways to customize tmux, I stumbled upon several more useful key remaps, which I decided to use:
# split panes using | and -
bind
|
split-window -h
bind
- split-window -v
unbind
'"'
unbind %
# reload config file (change file location to your the tmux.conf you want to use)
bind
r source-file ~/.tmux.conf
;
display-message
"~/.tmux.conf reloaded."
# switch panes using Alt-arrow without prefix
bind
-n M-Left
select
-pane -L
bind
-n M-Right
select
-pane -R
bind
-n M-Up
select
-pane -U
bind
-n M-Down
select
44787374.article_summary: 本文介绍了终端复用工具tmux的功能和使用体验。tmux允许在一个终端中运行多个终端会话，支持创建多个窗口和窗格，便于同时管理不同项目。其主要功能包括保护远程服务器上的运行程序免受连接中断影响，以及从多台本地计算机访问远程程序。尽管初始界面不友好且快捷键繁多，但tmux高度可定制，用户可通过编辑`.tmux.conf`文件调整设置，如更改前缀键、分割窗格的快捷键，以及无需前缀键切换窗格等。尽管初始体验不佳，但其强大的定制功能使其成为高效管理终端会话的有力工具。

data.title: Three weeks after acquiring Windsurf, Cognition offers staff the exit door
data.author: ABS
data.article_summary: AI coding startup Cognition, which acquired Windsurf three weeks ago, recently laid off 30 employees and offered buyouts to the remaining 200. This follows a turbulent period for Windsurf, which previously nearly merged with OpenAI, lost key executives and talent to Google, and was ultimately acquired by Cognition. Despite initial promises of financial compensation and excitement over Windsurf's talent, it's now clear the acquisition focused on the company's intellectual property. Employees have until August 10 to accept a buyout of nine months' salary, while those staying must work over 80-hour weeks, reflecting harsh conditions common in the AI industry.
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Windsurf公司的知识产权价值以及收购行为的性质

不同观点：
• [Havoc的观点]  
Havoc质疑Windsurf是否拥有深厚的知识产权，认为除了员工的知识和品牌名称外，Windsurf并没有太多有价值的知识产权，特别是在专利方面并不丰富。Havoc提到，Windsurf的成功似乎更多依赖于员工的技能和经验（"Just know how"），而不是专利技术。此外，Havoc指出公司解雇了一些员工，暗示公司在管理或战略上可能存在问题。

• [schwentkerr的观点]  
schwentkerr提出了“Windsurf Paradox”（风帆冲浪悖论）的概念，并撰写了一篇文章（链接已提供）讨论收购行为。schwentkerr认为，Windsurf的收购表面上看似是一种扩张或增强，但实际上更像是一种资源提取。这表明schwentkerr对收购行为的动机和后果持批评态度，可能认为收购方更多是在利用Windsurf的现有资源，而非真正看重其未来潜力。

补充讨论：
• [关于知识产权的争议]  
Havoc认为Windsurf的知识产权有限，主要集中在员工的知识和品牌名称，而schwentkerr则隐含了对公司被收购后资源利用方式的质疑，二者都对Windsurf的价值和收购的合理性提出了不同角度的看法。

• [员工被解雇的问题]  
Havoc特别提到公司解雇员工的问题，这可能是争议的一个焦点，表明公司内部可能存在管理和人力资源方面的问题，这也可能是schwentkerr批评收购行为的一个背景因素。

• [对收购的不同解读]  
Havoc对Windsurf的评论更集中在知识产权和员工知识的讨论上，而schwentkerr则从更广泛的角度，即“Windsurf Paradox”来分析收购行为，认为这是一种资源提取，而不是真正的价值提升。

整体来看，讨论围绕Windsurf的知识产权价值以及收购行为的动机和后果展开，不同观点对公司价值和收购的合理性提出了质疑。

44809084.article_content:
Cognition, the AI coding startup that acquired rival company Windsurf three weeks ago, laid off 30 employees last week and is offering buyouts to the roughly 200 remaining employees on the team,
reports The Information
.
This is the latest bout of whiplash that Windsurf employees have faced after a tumultuous stretch for the company. The startup was initially almost acquired by OpenAI, then lost its
CEO, co-founder, and research leads to Google
in a $2.4 billion deal known as a reverse-acquihire (where Google hired the key talent rather than buying the company), before ultimately getting
acquired by Cognition
.
At the time of the acquisition, Cognition stated that 100% of Windsurf employees would receive financial compensation as part of the deal and
stressed
that the company was excited to bring on Windsurf’s “world-class people” to develop top-notch coding tools.
Now, it’s becoming clear that Windsurf’s intellectual property, not its talent, was the real buy.
According to an email The Information viewed, employees were given until August 10 to decide whether they want to take the buyout, which amounts to nine months of salary. Those who choose to stay are reportedly required to spend six days at the office and clock more than 80-hour weeks — draconian conditions that have become
table stakes among workers at top AI firms.
“We don’t believe in work-life balance—building the future of software engineering is a mission we all care so deeply about that we couldn’t possibly separate the two,” wrote Cognition CEO Scott Wu in the email.
TechCrunch has reached out to Cognition for more details.

data.title: Hiroshima (1946)
data.author: pseudolus
data.article_summary: 1945年8月6日上午8点15分，广岛上空原子弹爆炸时，主人公们正处于日常生活中不同场景。东亚锡厂的职员佐佐木俊子刚在办公室坐下，医生藤井正一在私人医院的走廊上读报纸，寡妇中村初代在厨房观察邻居拆房，神父克莱茵佐尔格在教会宿舍休息，医生佐佐木辉夫在医院走廊拿血液样本，牧师谷本清利在城郊准备卸下手推车物品。十万人在原子弹爆炸中丧生，而他们幸存下来。他们不明白为何自己能活下来，回想许多偶然的细节让他们幸免于难。谷本牧师那天清晨五点起床，因连夜空袭警告而疲惫不堪。他 evacuated 教会的物品到郊区以防空袭。尽管身心俱疲，他仍早起帮助朋友搬运物品。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：广岛和长崎原子弹轰炸的必要性、伦理问题以及历史叙述

不同观点：
• **支持轰炸的观点**：
  - [throw0101d] 引用《140 Days to Hiroshima》一书，指出日本领导层在原子弹投下后仍不愿投降，甚至发生了阻止投降广播的未遂政变（京都事件），表明即使在原子弹投下后，日本的投降也并非立即或必然。
  - [karlgkk] 认为美国领导人对日本平民伤亡相对不关心，是因为日本在珍珠港事件及战争中的暴行使美国人对日本的敌意加深，且杜鲁门总统对使用原子弹的决定也与战争的长期影响和亲身经历有关。
  - [Pooge] 认为如果日本先拥有原子弹，他们也会毫不犹豫地使用。同时指出如果战争继续，日本的"樱花行动"可能带来更大的灾难，如传播鼠疫。而东京的燃烧弹轰炸比原子弹造成的伤亡更大。

• **反对轰炸或质疑其必要性的观点**：
  - [defrost] 指出对许多广岛人来说，原子弹轰炸只是一连串城市轰炸中的一个，与其他被轰炸的城市类似。这表明轰炸的独特性更多是被外界夸大，而当地人对其的反应相对冷漠。
  - [sgnelson] 提到关于是否应投放原子弹的争论会一直存在，并指出美国政府曾试图掩盖广岛和长崎的许多事实，以隐藏核武器的真正影响。
  - [wouterjanl] 质疑人们是否因国家立场而忽视了原子弹轰炸背后的人类苦难，并提出是否应将轰炸视为“必要”或“合理”的讨论是国家主义思维的体现。
  - [forinti] 认为将焦点放在广岛和长崎可能低估了整个轰炸行动的广泛悲剧性，因为其他城市的燃烧弹轰炸也同样旨在伤害平民。

• **关于历史叙述与媒体作用的观点**：
  - [cypherpunks01] 提到《纽约客》全刊发表的《广岛》一文，旨在让公众了解原子弹的毁灭性力量及其对人类的影响，显示出媒体在揭示真相和引导公众讨论中的重要作用。
  - [_rm] 则从写作风格的角度，指出过去与现代媒体在处理此类悲剧事件时的不同叙述方式。

补充讨论：
• **关于原子弹威力与现代核武器的比较**：
  - [thomasfl] 指出今天的核武器威力比投放在广岛的原子弹大80倍，因此难以再为使用如此强大的武器辩护。

• **关于历史假设与决策困难**：
  - [Isamu] 提到日本领导层内部的分裂使得战争结束的决策复杂化，并指出难以证明如果不投下原子弹是否会导致更多或更少的死亡。

争议焦点：
• 轰炸的伦理问题：是否应以战争罪行或军事必要性来合理化对平民的巨大伤害。
• 历史叙述的选择性：媒体和政府在呈现和掩盖某些事实中的角色对公众理解历史事件的影响。
• 现代核武器的威胁：如何看待现代核武器的威力以及过去决策的伦理问题。

I—A Noiseless Flash
At exactly fifteen minutes past eight in the morning, on August 6, 1945, Japanese time, at the moment when the atomic bomb flashed above Hiroshima, Miss Toshiko Sasaki, a clerk in the personnel department of the East Asia Tin Works, had just sat down at her place in the plant office and was turning her head to speak to the girl at the next desk. At that same moment, Dr. Masakazu Fujii was settling down cross-legged to read the Osaka
Asahi
on the porch of his private hospital, overhanging one of the seven deltaic rivers which divide Hiroshima; Mrs. Hatsuyo Nakamura, a tailor’s widow, stood by the window of her kitchen, watching a neighbor tearing down his house because it lay in the path of an air-raid-defense fire lane; Father Wilhelm Kleinsorge, a German priest of the Society of Jesus, reclined in his underwear on a cot on the top floor of his order’s three-story mission house, reading a Jesuit magazine,
Stimmen der Zeit
; Dr. Terufumi Sasaki, a young member of the surgical staff of the city’s large, modern Red Cross Hospital, walked along one of the hospital corridors with a blood specimen for a Wassermann test in his hand; and the Reverend Mr. Kiyoshi Tanimoto, pastor of the Hiroshima Methodist Church, paused at the door of a rich man’s house in Koi, the city’s western suburb, and prepared to unload a handcart full of things he had evacuated from town in fear of the massive B-29 raid which everyone expected Hiroshima to suffer. A hundred thousand people were killed by the atomic bomb, and these six were among the survivors. They still wonder why they lived when so many others died. Each of them counts many small items of chance or volition—a step taken in time, a decision to go indoors, catching one streetcar instead of the next—that spared him. And now each knows that in the act of survival he lived a dozen lives and saw more death than he ever thought he would see. At the time, none of them knew anything.
The Reverend Mr. Tanimoto got up at five o’clock that morning. He was alone in the parsonage, because for some time his wife had been commuting with their year-old baby to spend nights with a friend in Ushida, a suburb to the north. Of all the important cities of Japan, only two, Kyoto and Hiroshima, had not been visited in strength by
B-san

He had heard uncomfortably detailed accounts of mass raids on Kure, Iwakuni, Tokuyama, and other nearby towns; he was sure Hiroshima’s turn would come soon. He had slept badly the night before, because there had been several air-raid warnings. Hiroshima had been getting such warnings almost every night for weeks, for at that time the B-29s were using Lake Biwa, northeast of Hiroshima, as a rendezvous point, and no matter what city the Americans planned to hit, the Super-fortresses streamed in over the coast near Hiroshima. The frequency of the warnings and the continued abstinence of Mr. B with respect to Hiroshima had made its citizens jittery; a rumor was going around that the Americans were saving something special for the city.
Mr. Tanimoto is a small man, quick to talk, laugh, and cry. He wears his black hair parted in the middle and rather long; the prominence of the frontal bones just above his eyebrows and the smallness of his mustache, mouth, and chin give him a strange, old-young look, boyish and yet wise, weak and yet fiery. He moves nervously and fast, but with a restraint which suggests that he is a cautious, thoughtful man. He showed, indeed, just those qualities in the uneasy days before the bomb fell. Besides having his wife spend the nights in Ushida, Mr. Tanimoto had been carrying all the portable things from his church, in the close-packed residential district called Nagaragawa, to a house that belonged to a rayon manufacturer in Koi, two miles from the center of town. The rayon man, a Mr. Matsui, had opened his then unoccupied estate to a large number of his friends and acquaintances, so that they might evacuate whatever they wished to a safe distance from the probable target area. Mr. Tanimoto had had no difficulty in moving chairs, hymnals, Bibles, altar gear, and church records by pushcart himself, but the organ console and an upright piano required some aid. A friend of his named Matsuo had, the day before, helped him get the piano out to Koi; in return, he had promised this day to assist Mr. Matsuo in hauling out a daughter’s belongings. That is why he had risen so early.

44766551.article_summary: 1945年8月6日上午8点15分，广岛上空原子弹爆炸时，主人公们正处于日常生活中不同场景。东亚锡厂的职员佐佐木俊子刚在办公室坐下，医生藤井正一在私人医院的走廊上读报纸，寡妇中村初代在厨房观察邻居拆房，神父克莱茵佐尔格在教会宿舍休息，医生佐佐木辉夫在医院走廊拿血液样本，牧师谷本清利在城郊准备卸下手推车物品。十万人在原子弹爆炸中丧生，而他们幸存下来。他们不明白为何自己能活下来，回想许多偶然的细节让他们幸免于难。谷本牧师那天清晨五点起床，因连夜空袭警告而疲惫不堪。他 evacuated 教会的物品到郊区以防空袭。尽管身心俱疲，他仍早起帮助朋友搬运物品。
